display.title: You Do Your Best and Hashem Does the Rest
display.summary_short: Lessons in bitachon from Chanukah, and a Chassid who braves a snowstorm to reach the Baal Shem Tov's Melave Malka and is given a ride by a singing wagon driver.
display.summary_long: After the song "I believe in Hashem", the storyteller draws the lesson of Chanukah: the few and weak Chashmonaim trusted in Hashem against the many and mighty. He tells how the Rebbe asked a visiting professor to name the greatest miracle in history; the answer is that the Jewish people still exist, thanks to the eternal Torah. Bitachon still means doing our part, like going to a doctor or working for a living, while knowing that the result comes from Hashem. Introducing a story about the Baal Shem Tov's Melave Malka, he explains 'accompanying' a guest, sharing his own childhood memories of watching the Rebbe walk his mother, Rebbetzin Chana, out of 770, and of holding the heavy door of her building open for her. He explains why Melave Malka is Dovid HaMelech's meal. The story: Reb Moshe never misses the Baal Shem Tov's Melave Malka in Mezhibuzh, a short walk through a forest from his town. One Motzaei Shabbos, in a blizzard, he falls into a muddy pit, goes home to change, and sets out again. A pots-and-pans peddler offers him a ride and they sing zemiros together. At the table the Baal Shem Tov asks him to tell everyone what it felt like to sing zemiros with Eliyahu HaNavi.
display.lesson: When you want to do something good and it is hard, try anyway: you do your best, and Hashem does the rest.
